title: Numb, painful feet in a 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes
desc: This station involves a focused history and neurological and foot examination of a 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who has six months of symmetrical numbness and shooting pain in both feet and feels unsteady. The candidate then interprets his neuropathy bloods, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and diabetes foot assessment, and plans glycaemic control, foot protection, falls prevention and safety netting.
focus: Altered sensation in the feet: recognising and working up diabetic peripheral neuropathy, and managing foot and falls risk in general practice
diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes with poor glycaemic control
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in a general practice. Patrick Doyle, a 63-year-old man, has come to see you because his feet have been "feeling a bit funny". Your GP supervisor will see him after you.
tasks: Take a focused history from Patrick and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Patrick's blood results, his urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and the practice nurse's diabetes foot assessment. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Patrick Doyle, a 63-year-old retired chef. You are friendly and a bit puzzled. You play the symptoms down until someone asks about falling, and then your real worry comes out. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "It's really weird, doctor. My feet have been feeling a bit funny lately. I just wanted to get it checked to make sure it's nothing serious."

The feet (give only when asked):

  • Where: both feet, the same on each side: the toes, the soles and the tops. It has crept up into the lower legs. Your hands are fine.
  • What it feels like: mostly numbness, "like walking on cotton wool". Recently you have had an occasional sharp, shooting pain.
  • Timing: the numbness came on gradually about 6 months ago. It came and went at first but is now more frequent. The shooting pain is recent and has happened three times so far.
  • Severity: if asked, the pain is 5 out of 10.
  • What changes it: nothing makes it better or worse.
  • Other sensations: no pins and needles, tingling or burning.

Other neurological symptoms:

  • Your lower legs feel a bit weak. You feel unsteady on your feet at times, especially in the dark, but you have not fallen.
  • No back pain. No problems controlling your bladder or bowels. No numbness around your bottom or between your legs.
  • No headache, change in vision or hearing, trouble swallowing or change in speech.
  • No dizziness when you stand up, no feeling full early when eating, and no problems with erections.

Feet and circulation: no sores or ulcers on your feet, and the shape of your feet has not changed. No pain in the calves when walking.

Past medical history: type 2 diabetes since age 55, high cholesterol and high blood pressure. If asked: you have never had low vitamin B12, haemochromatosis, back problems, multiple sclerosis or Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Medicines:

  • If asked what you take: "Metformin, atorvastatin and lisinopril."
  • Only if asked how often you take them, or whether you have any side effects: "I don't take the metformin very often because I get diarrhoea and that makes me feel very sick." You take it only now and then, and you have not told anyone.
  • You take the atorvastatin and lisinopril every day.

Allergies: none.

Family history: your father died of a heart attack at 53, and your mother had a stroke at 65.

Social history:

  • Retired chef. You live with your wife, and your two sons are supportive.
  • Ex-smoker: a pack a day for 20 years, quit 10 years ago.
  • Alcohol: an occasional can of beer on weekends.
  • Diet: you eat meat and dairy, and you are not vegetarian or vegan.
  • You often walk barefoot around the house (if asked about footwear).

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: you think it is part of getting old.
  • Concern (say this when asked how it affects you, or about falls): "I feel a bit unsteady on my feet at times. I'm worried I'm going to fall and break my bones and won't be able to help my wife."
  • Expectation: you want to know it is nothing serious.

Question to raise once your concerns have been explored: "Is this just part of getting old, doctor?"

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they examine):

  • General and observations: comfortable, overweight. BP 142/86 mmHg sitting and 138/84 mmHg after 3 minutes standing (no postural drop). HR 74/min regular. Temperature 36.6 °C. Weight 96 kg, height 176 cm, BMI 31 kg/m². Capillary glucose 11.2 mmol/L (random).
  • Feet, shoes and socks off: dry skin on both feet, with mild callus under the first metatarsal heads on both sides. No ulcers, fissures or infection. No deformity, no midfoot collapse, and the feet are not hot or swollen. Nails normal. Wearing worn, thin-soled slip-on shoes.
  • Circulation: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable on both sides. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Feet warm, normal hair.
  • Sensation in the lower limbs:
    • 10 g monofilament not felt at the plantar forefoot sites on either foot.
    • Vibration (128 Hz tuning fork) absent at both great toes, reduced at the medial malleoli and normal at the knees.
    • Joint position sense impaired at both great toes and normal at the ankles.
    • Pinprick reduced symmetrically from the toes to mid-shin on both sides, in a stocking distribution.
  • Upper limbs: sensation, power and reflexes normal.
  • Tone, power and reflexes in the lower limbs: tone normal. Mild weakness of great toe extension on both sides (MRC 4+/5); otherwise 5/5. Ankle reflexes absent on both sides, even with reinforcement. Knee reflexes present, normal (not brisk) and equal. Plantar responses flexor. No clonus. No wasting or fasciculation.
  • Gait and balance: gait slightly broad-based. Unsteady on heel-to-toe (tandem) walking. Romberg test positive: steady with eyes open, sways and needs to step with eyes closed.
  • Back: no spinal tenderness. Straight leg raise negative on both sides.

part2.lead: When Patrick booked last week he mentioned his feet, so the GP ordered fasting bloods, including a neuropathy screen, and a urine ACR alongside his diabetes review. The practice nurse completed his diabetes foot assessment today before you saw him. Here are the results.
part2.patient:
• When the candidate explains the diagnosis, ask: "So it's not just old age? Will the feeling come back?"
  • When metformin comes up: "I really can't stand that tablet. The diarrhoea is awful. Do I have to keep taking it?" Be relieved if a different form or another option is offered, and admit you have been taking it only now and then.
  • If falls are not addressed, ask: "What can I do so I don't fall over?"

handover.label: Bloods (last week, fasting)
handover.result: Fasting sample, collected at 08:10. Lab comment: HbA1c above the general treatment target for diabetes.
handover.model:
• Read: HbA1c 8.9% (74 mmol/mol) and fasting glucose 9.8 mmol/L, both well above the general target of 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or less. FBC normal, including MCV 89. B12 320 pmol/L and folate normal. TSH normal. LFTs and GGT normal. No paraprotein. eGFR 72.
  • For Patrick: his glycaemic control is poor, which fits his admission that he takes metformin only now and then. This is the main driver of his neuropathy. The normal B12, folate and MCV make B12 deficiency unlikely. The normal TSH excludes hypothyroidism. A normal GGT fits his low alcohol intake. No paraprotein. An eGFR of 72 is far too high for uraemic neuropathy.
  • What it changes: the treatable mimics are excluded, so this is diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Glycaemic control needs fixing by tackling his metformin intolerance. B12 still needs checking periodically while he takes metformin.

rows.n: 60-89 is CKD only if kidney damage is present
General target in diabetes 7.0% or less
General target in diabetes 53 or less

handover.label: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
handover.result: Early morning (first void) urine, collected last week. Lab comment: raised albumin excretion; confirm with repeat samples.
handover.model:
• Read: the uACR of 4.2 mg/mmol is above the male reference of under 2.5, in the moderately increased range (microalbuminuria). Combined with an eGFR of 72, this is CKD stage G2 A2 if it persists.
  • For Patrick: this probably shows early diabetic kidney disease, another microvascular complication alongside the neuropathy. It needs confirming: at least 2 of 3 samples raised over 3 months. It is far too mild to cause a uraemic neuropathy.
  • What it changes: continue lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor protects the kidneys) and titrate to the maximum tolerated dose (check potassium and creatinine 1-2 weeks after each increase) to reach BP 130/80 mmHg or less; his BP today is 142/86. Favour an SGLT2 inhibitor as the second glucose-lowering agent, and add one once repeat samples confirm the albuminuria, whatever the HbA1c. Repeat the uACR, and check eGFR and uACR at least yearly.

rows.n: Concentration shown for calculation; interpret the ACR
Repeat to confirm: 2 of 3 samples over 3 months

handover.label: Diabetes foot assessment (practice nurse)
handover.result:
Diabetes foot assessment, annual cycle of care, done by the practice nurse today.

History: no previous foot ulcer, amputation or Charcot foot. Not on dialysis. No claudication or rest pain.

Inspection: dry skin on both feet. Mild callus under the first metatarsal heads on both sides. No ulcer, fissure, infection or pre-ulcerative lesion. No deformity. Nails normal.

Footwear: worn, thin-soled slip-on shoes with poor support. Patrick reports often walking barefoot at home.

Neurological: 10 g monofilament not felt at the plantar forefoot sites on either foot. 128 Hz tuning fork absent at both great toes. Ankle reflexes absent on both sides.

Vascular: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable on both sides. Doppler waveforms triphasic. Ankle-brachial index: right 1.08, left 1.04.

Conclusion: Loss of protective sensation in both feet. No peripheral arterial disease. No deformity and no history of ulceration. Podiatry review recommended for the callus and footwear.
handover.model:
• Read: the feet cannot feel the monofilament and vibration is absent at the great toes: loss of protective sensation. Both ABIs are normal (0.9 to 1.3) with triphasic waveforms, so there is no peripheral arterial disease. There is mild callus but no ulcer or deformity, and he has never had an ulcer. His footwear is poor and he walks barefoot.
  • For Patrick: this confirms a sensory neuropathy with an at-risk foot. Arterial disease is excluded as the cause of his symptoms. The risk category is IWGDG risk 1, which the Australian guideline (Diabetes Feet Australia 2021) classes as intermediate risk.
  • What it changes: foot review at least every 6 to 12 months (many practices review every 3 to 6 months), with podiatry for the callus and footwear, and education: check his feet daily, never walk barefoot, wear protective footwear and test water temperature. Mild callus under the metatarsal heads of an insensate foot shows high plantar pressure and raises ulcer risk, so podiatry debridement and offloading footwear matter.

ask: You are now handing over to your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of Patrick Doyle, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Patrick now, here in general practice.
Before Patrick goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student; Patrick Doyle, 63.
  • Situation: 6 months of progressive symmetrical numbness in both feet, recent shooting pains and unsteadiness. No falls.
  • Background: type 2 diabetes for 8 years. Rarely takes metformin because of diarrhoea. Hypertension and high cholesterol, on lisinopril and atorvastatin. Ex-smoker (20 pack-years). Minimal alcohol.
  • Assessment: stocking sensory loss to mid-shin, absent ankle reflexes, Romberg positive. HbA1c 8.9% (74). B12, folate, MCV, TSH, LFTs and SPEP normal. uACR 4.2 with eGFR 72. Foot assessment: loss of protective sensation, ABI normal, IWGDG risk 1 (Australian intermediate risk), needing foot review at least every 6 to 12 months (many practices review every 3 to 6 months), with podiatry. Likely diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
  • Recommendation: review metformin (extended release), podiatry, physiotherapy for falls, repeat uACR, review in 4 weeks.

Most likely: diabetic peripheral neuropathy (distal symmetrical sensorimotor). For: 8 years of diabetes with HbA1c 8.9%, gradual symmetrical stocking loss of all sensory modalities, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg, and normal results for the treatable mimics.

  • B12 deficiency: metformin is a risk. Against: he rarely takes it, he is not vegetarian, and his B12 and MCV are normal.
  • Alcohol-related neuropathy: against: only an occasional beer and a normal GGT.
  • Hypothyroidism: against: normal TSH.
  • CKD (uraemic) neuropathy: against: eGFR 72 is far too high.
  • Spinal cord compression: against: no upper motor neuron signs (flexor plantars, no clonus, normal tone, knee reflexes not brisk) and no sensory level.
  • Cauda equina compression: against: no back pain, no sphincter or saddle symptoms, and a gradual, symmetrical, length-dependent stocking pattern rather than a saddle or radicular pattern.

1. Explain: nerve damage from high blood sugar, not just ageing. Good control slows it down but may not reverse it.
  2. Glucose: target HbA1c 7.0% (53) or less, individualised. Switch to metformin XR, start low and titrate slowly. If HbA1c is still above target at 3 months, or he cannot tolerate it, add or switch to a second agent, favouring an SGLT2 inhibitor because of the albuminuria; add an SGLT2 inhibitor anyway once repeat samples confirm the albuminuria. Refer to a diabetes educator and a dietitian.
  3. Feet: podiatry referral (callus, footwear) under a GP chronic condition management plan.
  4. Falls: physiotherapy for strength and balance, home safety advice, good lighting at night and avoiding sedating medicines.
  5. Pain: infrequent at present. If it becomes troublesome, amitriptyline, pregabalin or duloxetine at a low dose, watching for dizziness and falls.
  6. Kidneys and heart: continue lisinopril and titrate to the maximum tolerated dose (check potassium and creatinine 1-2 weeks after each increase) to reach BP 130/80 or less; continue atorvastatin; repeat uACR; retinal screening.

• Feet: check them every day, using a mirror or his wife. Never walk barefoot. Wear supportive, well-fitting shoes. Test bath water with his elbow. Moisturise, but not between the toes.
  • See the GP within a day: any cut, blister, sore or new redness on a foot.
  • A hot, red or swollen foot, even without pain or fever (possible active Charcot foot): same-day GP review and urgent referral to the high-risk foot service; keep weight off the foot until assessed.
  • Go to ED: a hot swollen foot with fever or spreading redness, or a cold, pale or very painful foot.
  • Go to ED urgently (000 if severe): weakness or numbness spreading quickly over days (including into the hands), new difficulty walking, or new back pain with bladder or bowel problems or numbness around the bottom. A fall with injury needs prompt review.
  • Book a GP review: gradual new numbness in the hands.
  • Follow-up: review in 4 weeks for metformin tolerance. HbA1c in 3 months. Podiatry and physiotherapy appointments. Foot review at least every 6 to 12 months (many practices review every 3 to 6 months). Written information.

ddx.dx: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy)
ddx.for: Eight years of type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.9% from metformin non-adherence, gradual symmetrical stocking sensory loss to mid-shin, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg and loss of protective sensation.
Prescribed metformin for 8 years, with impaired vibration and joint position sense.
ddx.against: He rarely takes the metformin, he is not vegetarian or vegan, and his B12, folate and MCV are normal.

ddx.for: A length-dependent sensory neuropathy is the typical pattern.
ddx.against: He drinks only an occasional can of beer on weekends, and his GGT, LFTs and MCV are normal.

ddx.for: A treatable cause of symmetrical distal neuropathy in an older adult.
ddx.against: His TSH is 1.8 and he has no other features of hypothyroidism.

ddx.dx: Uraemic neuropathy from chronic kidney disease
ddx.for: His uACR of 4.2 mg/mmol suggests early diabetic kidney disease.
ddx.against: His eGFR of 72 is far too high to cause a uraemic neuropathy.

ddx.dx: Spinal cord or cauda equina compression
ddx.for: Bilateral leg symptoms with weakness and unsteadiness.
ddx.against: Against cord compression: no upper motor neuron signs (flexor plantars, no clonus, normal tone, knee reflexes not brisk) and no sensory level; against cauda equina: no back pain, no sphincter or saddle symptoms, and a gradual symmetrical stocking pattern rather than a saddle or radicular one.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, clear introduction and role, confirms Patrick's identity, and explains and gains consent for the examination, including removing shoes and socks.
Empathic and non-judgemental: acknowledges his fear of falling and of not being able to help his wife, does not blame him for skipping metformin, and uses plain language.
History
Characterises the altered sensation:

kids.x: Site and spread: both feet (toes, soles and tops), spreading into the lower legs, hands spared.
Onset and course: gradual over 6 months, intermittent at first and now more frequent.
Character and severity: numbness, with occasional sharp shooting pain (three episodes, 5/10).
Aggravating and relieving factors: nothing changes it.

check.x: Asks about positive sensory symptoms: pins and needles, tingling, burning [no pins and needles, tingling or burning; shooting pain as already described].
Asks about weakness, unsteadiness and falls [lower legs feel weak, unsteady at times, no falls].
Screens for red flags of a central or spinal cause: back pain, bladder or bowel incontinence, saddle numbness, headache, change in vision, hearing, speech or swallowing [all absent].
Asks about autonomic involvement: dizziness on standing, early satiety, erectile dysfunction [none].
Asks about foot and vascular complications: foot ulcers, change in foot shape (midfoot collapse), calf claudication [none].

Takes the past medical history: type 2 diabetes since 55, hypertension, high cholesterol, and asks about conditions relevant to neuropathy (e.g. B12 deficiency, thyroid, back problems, previous neurological illness) [none].
Takes a medication history including adherence, and finds he rarely takes metformin because of diarrhoea; also atorvastatin and lisinopril, and no allergies.
Asks about risk factors for other causes of neuropathy:

kids.x: Alcohol intake, quantified [an occasional can of beer on weekends].
Diet, including vegetarian or vegan diet, as a B12 risk [neither].

check.x: Takes a family and social history: father died of a heart attack at 53, mother had a stroke at 65; ex-smoker of 20 pack-years who quit 10 years ago; retired chef living with his wife, two supportive sons.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is part of getting old, fears falling and breaking bones and not being able to help his wife, and wants to know it is nothing serious.
Examination
Asks for observations, including lying or sitting and standing BP (no postural drop), BMI and a capillary glucose.

Inspects both feet with shoes and socks off: skin, callus, ulcers, deformity or Charcot changes, nails and footwear [dry skin, mild callus under the first metatarsal heads, no ulcer or deformity, worn shoes].
Palpates the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses and checks capillary refill and temperature [all normal].
Performs a lower limb sensory examination, distal to proximal, comparing both sides:

kids.x: 10 g monofilament on the plantar foot [not felt on either foot].
Vibration with a 128 Hz tuning fork from the great toe upwards [absent at the toes, reduced at the malleoli].
Joint position sense at the great toe [impaired].
Pinprick to map the level and pattern, and compares with the hands [stocking to mid-shin, hands normal].

check.x: Examines tone, power and reflexes in the lower limbs, including ankle and knee reflexes and plantar responses [mild great toe extension weakness, absent ankles, knees present and not brisk, plantars flexor].
Assesses gait, tandem walking and Romberg's test [broad-based, unsteady tandem walking, Romberg positive].
Briefly examines the back [no tenderness, straight leg raise negative].
Interpretation
Interprets HbA1c 8.9% (74 mmol/mol) and fasting glucose 9.8 mmol/L as poor glycaemic control, well above the general target of 7.0% (53) or less, and links it to his metformin non-adherence.
States that the normal B12, folate and MCV make B12 deficiency unlikely, and that B12 still needs periodic checks while he takes metformin.
States that the normal TSH, LFTs and GGT, and the absence of a paraprotein, are against hypothyroidism, alcohol and a paraproteinaemic neuropathy.
Interprets uACR 4.2 mg/mmol with eGFR 72 as albuminuria suggesting early diabetic kidney disease, which needs repeat samples to confirm and is far too mild to cause uraemic neuropathy.

Interprets the foot assessment: loss of protective sensation, normal ABI so no peripheral arterial disease, no ulcer or deformity, so IWGDG risk 1 (Australian intermediate risk), needing regular foot review (every 6 to 12 months, or 3 to 6 months is accepted) and podiatry.

Gives diabetic peripheral neuropathy as the most likely diagnosis, justified by the symmetrical stocking sensory loss, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg, poor control and normal results for the mimics.
Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: B12 deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism, CKD, and spinal cord or cauda equina compression.
Management
Explains in plain language that this is nerve damage from high blood sugar rather than just getting older, and that better control slows progression but may not bring the feeling back.
Plans better glycaemic control:

kids.x: Agrees an individualised HbA1c target (generally 7.0% or 53 mmol/mol or less).
Addresses the intolerance: switches to extended-release metformin (or takes it with meals), starting low and titrating slowly.

Adds or switches to a second agent if HbA1c is still above target at 3 months or metformin is not tolerated, or once albuminuria is confirmed, favouring an SGLT2 inhibitor because of the albuminuria; refers to a diabetes educator and dietitian.

check.x: Plans foot protection: refers to podiatry for the callus and footwear under a GP chronic condition management plan.
Addresses falls risk: physiotherapy for strength and balance, home safety advice (lighting at night), and avoiding sedating medicines where possible.
check.d: Award for physiotherapy plus any one home-safety or medicine-review measure.

check.x: Gives a plan for neuropathic pain if it becomes troublesome: amitriptyline, pregabalin or duloxetine started at a low dose, with a warning that dizziness and sedation add to his falls risk.
Repeats the uACR, continues and uptitrates lisinopril towards BP 130/80 or less, continues atorvastatin and arranges retinal screening.
Safety netting

Teaches daily foot checks and no barefoot walking, and names foot red flags: a cut, blister, sore or new redness needs GP review within a day; a hot, red or swollen foot needs same-day review and the high-risk foot service (possible Charcot); fever or spreading redness, or a cold, pale or very painful foot, needs ED.
Names neurological red flags: rapidly spreading weakness or numbness, new difficulty walking, or new back pain with bladder/bowel problems or saddle numbness needs ED urgently.
Arranges follow-up: review in about 4 weeks for metformin tolerance, HbA1c in 3 months, foot review every 3 to 12 months (either guideline interval accepted), written information.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Patrick reveals the metformin problem only when asked directly how he takes his tablets, and his fear of falling only when asked about falls or how it affects him. In Part 2 the examiner hands over all three results together and asks the four questions in order. The person playing Patrick puts his Part 2 questions while the candidate explains.

Foot review interval: accept either 6 to 12 months (Diabetes Feet Australia 2021 / IWGDG risk 1) or 3 to 6 months (RACGP handbook intermediate risk); the candidate does not need to name the source.

A high-performing candidate maps a symmetrical stocking pattern, separates positive from negative symptoms, screens for spinal and central red flags and autonomic symptoms, and uncovers the metformin non-adherence. They examine the feet with shoes off, use the monofilament and tuning fork, test reflexes and Romberg, and check pulses. In Part 2 they link the HbA1c to the non-adherence and use the normal results to exclude B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism and alcohol. They note the albuminuria and classify the foot risk. They then offer extended-release metformin or a second agent, podiatry, falls prevention and specific red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic history and misses the adherence problem or the falls concern. They do not remove the shoes, omit the monofilament, or say "neuropathy" without justifying it. They reassure Patrick that it is just age, tell him to "take your metformin" without addressing the diarrhoea, or give vague safety netting such as "come back if worse".
explain:
Describing altered sensation

Sensory symptoms are positive (tingling, pins and needles, burning, tightness, shooting pain) or negative (numbness, loss of feeling). The distribution localises the lesion:

  • Glove and stocking: a length-dependent peripheral polyneuropathy, from diabetes, toxins including alcohol, drugs, infection, B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, CKD or a paraprotein.
  • Dermatomal: a root or cord lesion, such as a disc.
  • A single nerve territory: a nerve injury or compression.

Diabetic peripheral neuropathy

The commonest pattern is a distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy. It starts in the toes and climbs the legs before it reaches the hands, because the longest nerves are affected first. It causes:

  • numbness and neuropathic pain;
  • loss of protective sensation, vibration and joint position sense;
  • absent ankle reflexes with preserved knee reflexes;
  • sensory ataxia (unsteady in the dark, Romberg positive);
  • sometimes mild distal weakness.

Patrick has 8 years of type 2 diabetes, poor control (HbA1c 8.9%) because metformin gives him diarrhoea, and exactly this picture. Autonomic neuropathy (postural hypotension, gastroparesis with early satiety, erectile dysfunction) should be asked about, and he has none.

Differentials and the results

The treatable mimics must be excluded before the label is accepted:

  • B12 deficiency: a risk with long-term metformin and vegan diets. His B12, folate and MCV are normal.
  • Alcohol: he drinks little and his GGT is normal.
  • Hypothyroidism: his TSH is normal.
  • CKD: uraemic neuropathy needs advanced kidney disease, and his eGFR is 72.
  • Paraproteinaemia: the electrophoresis is negative.

No back pain, sphincter or saddle symptoms and the symmetrical stocking pattern argue against cauda equina compression; the absence of upper motor neuron signs (flexor plantars, no clonus, normal tone, knee reflexes not brisk) and of a sensory level argues against cord compression. Rapid progression, asymmetry, prominent weakness or early hand involvement should prompt nerve conduction studies and neurology referral. A typical presentation does not need them.

His uACR of 4.2 mg/mmol shows albuminuria, probably early diabetic kidney disease. It needs confirming on at least 2 of 3 samples over 3 months. The foot assessment shows loss of protective sensation with a normal ABI and no deformity or ulcer history: IWGDG risk 1, which the Australian guideline (Diabetes Feet Australia 2021) classes as intermediate risk. He needs foot review at least every 6 to 12 months (many practices review every 3 to 6 months), with podiatry.

Management

  • Glycaemic control: aim for an individualised HbA1c, generally 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or less. Good control slows progression of neuropathy but rarely reverses it. Metformin intolerance is common and can often be managed by taking it with meals, starting low and titrating slowly, or by changing to the extended-release form: metformin XR 500 mg once daily with the evening meal, increasing by 500 mg every 1 to 2 weeks as tolerated (usual maximum 2 g daily). If HbA1c remains above target, add a second agent. With albuminuria (and his cardiovascular risk), an SGLT2 inhibitor is favoured for its kidney and cardiovascular benefit. If repeat samples confirm persistent albuminuria (CKD G2 A2), add an SGLT2 inhibitor for kidney and cardiovascular protection regardless of HbA1c. Involve a diabetes educator and dietitian.
  • B12: check periodically while on metformin.
  • Feet: refer to podiatry (callus and footwear), using a GP chronic condition management plan for Medicare-subsidised visits. Teach daily self-inspection, no barefoot walking, protective footwear, testing water temperature and skin care.
  • Neuropathic pain: first-line options in eTG are amitriptyline, pregabalin (or gabapentin) and duloxetine, started at low doses and titrated. In an unsteady older man, sedation, dizziness and anticholinergic effects add to falls risk. Patrick's pain is infrequent, so drug treatment can wait until it is troublesome.
  • Falls: physiotherapy for strength and balance, home safety and good lighting, and a review of sedating medicines.
  • Other complications and cardiovascular risk: continue the ACE inhibitor and titrate it to the maximum tolerated dose (checking potassium and creatinine 1 to 2 weeks after each increase), continue the statin, aim for BP 130/80 mmHg or less with albuminuria, and arrange retinal screening and the rest of the annual cycle of care.

Safety netting

Loss of protective sensation means a foot injury can go unnoticed. Any cut, blister, sore or new redness needs a GP review within a day. A hot, red or swollen foot, even without pain or fever (possible active Charcot foot), needs same-day GP review and urgent referral to the high-risk foot service; he should keep weight off the foot until assessed. A hot swollen foot with fever or spreading redness (possible infection), or a cold, pale or very painful foot (acute ischaemia), needs ED. Weakness or numbness spreading quickly over days (including into the hands), new difficulty walking, or new back pain with bladder or bowel problems or saddle numbness suggests a different, urgent diagnosis and needs ED urgently (000 if severe); a fall with injury needs prompt review. Gradual new numbness in the hands needs a booked GP review.
points: Glove-and-stocking sensory loss points to a length-dependent peripheral neuropathy, a dermatomal pattern to a root or cord lesion, and a single nerve territory to a nerve compression or injury.

Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is symmetrical and starts in the toes, with loss of protective sensation and vibration, absent ankle reflexes and sensory ataxia. Exclude the treatable mimics: B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, alcohol, CKD and a paraprotein.

Always ask how patients actually take their medicines. Metformin diarrhoea often means non-adherence, which can be managed with meals, slow titration, extended release or a second agent (an SGLT2 inhibitor is favoured with albuminuria).
Check B12 periodically in people on long-term metformin.

Loss of protective sensation makes an at-risk foot: arrange podiatry, teach daily foot checks and protective footwear, and arrange foot review at least every 6 to 12 months (many practices review every 3 to 6 months) when there is no PAD, deformity or ulcer history (IWGDG risk 1, Australian intermediate risk).
Neuropathic pain drugs (amitriptyline, pregabalin, duloxetine) start low, and their dizziness and sedation add to falls risk in someone already unsteady from sensory ataxia.
